note: Front lines and held areas are approximate reconstructions traced from US Army Center of Military History campaign maps; in the fluid campaigns of 1950 the 'front' joins separate columns across ground neither side held, and bypassed units and guerrillas behind the lines are not shown.

chapters.title: North Korea invades
arrows: North Korean drive on Seoul and Taejon
North Korean advance through the central mountains
North Korean advance down the east coast
North Korean 6th Division sweeps the south-west
chapters.text: Before dawn on 25 June 1950 the North Korean army crossed the 38th parallel with tanks and artillery. Seoul fell on 28 June, and the first US troops, rushed in from Japan, were pushed back at Osan on 5 July and at Taejon on 20 July. By early August the South Korean and UN forces had been driven into the south-east corner of the peninsula, behind the Naktong River.

chapters.title: The Pusan Perimeter
arrows: North Korean attack across the Naktong Bulge
North Korean attack towards Yongchon and P'ohang-dong
chapters.text: South Korean, US and newly arrived British troops held a line around the port of Pusan, with the Naktong River on its western side and mountains to the north. North Korean attacks crossed the river at the 'Naktong Bulge', pressed on Taegu and fought for P'ohang-dong on the east coast, but troops and supplies landed at Pusan let the defenders hold until mid-September.

chapters.title: Inchon and the breakout
arrows: Inchon landing and the drive on Seoul
Eighth Army breaks out of the Pusan Perimeter
chapters.text: On 15 September US Marines landed at Inchon, far behind the North Korean front. They took Kimpo airfield on 17–18 September and fought their way into Seoul, which was cleared by 28 September. Meanwhile the Eighth Army broke out of the Pusan Perimeter; its spearhead met troops from Inchon near Osan on 26–27 September, and the North Korean army fell apart and retreated north.

chapters.title: Across the 38th parallel to the Yalu
arrows: South Korean advance up the east coast
UN advance on Pyongyang
South Korean 6th Division reaches the Yalu
Chinese First Phase Offensive at Unsan
chapters.text: South Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel on 1 October and UN forces followed. Wonsan fell on 10 October, Hamhung on 17 October and Pyongyang on 19 October, and on 26 October a South Korean unit reached the Yalu River at Chosan, on the Chinese border. Chinese troops had secretly crossed the Yalu; they struck at Unsan in late October and then pulled back, and by 24 November the UN armies were again advancing towards the border.

chapters.title: China's offensive and the retreat
arrows: Chinese Second Phase Offensive on the Ch'ongch'on
Chinese attack at the Chosin Reservoir
Breakout from the Chosin Reservoir to Hungnam
Chinese Third Phase Offensive takes Seoul
chapters.text: On 25 November Chinese armies attacked in force. The Eighth Army was routed on the Ch'ongch'on River and abandoned Pyongyang in early December, while in the north-east US Marines fought their way out from the Chosin Reservoir to Hungnam, from which X Corps and more than 86,000 refugees were taken off by sea by 24 December. A new Chinese offensive took Seoul on 4 January 1951 and pushed the UN line south to near the 37th parallel.

chapters.title: Seoul retaken and the spring offensives
arrows: Operation Thunderbolt
Chinese offensive at Hoengsong
Operation Ripper retakes Seoul
Operation Ripper takes Chuncheon
Chinese spring offensive on the Imjin and at Kapyong
Chinese spring offensive in the east
UN counter-offensive to the Iron Triangle
UN counter-offensive in the east
chapters.text: From late January UN forces under General Matthew Ridgway advanced step by step, retaking Inchon in February and Seoul in mid-March, and crossed back over the 38th parallel. Chinese spring offensives in April and May drove them back towards Seoul and broke through in the east, but at huge cost. By mid-June UN forces held a line from the Imjin River through the base of the 'Iron Triangle' to the east coast, mostly north of the parallel.

chapters.title: Talks and the hill battles
arrows: Bloody Ridge and Heartbreak Ridge
Operation Commando
chapters.text: Armistice talks opened at Kaesong on 10 July 1951 and moved to Panmunjom in October. While they dragged on, stalled mainly over whether prisoners could refuse to go home, the front settled into lines of trenches and bunkers. Both sides fought costly battles for single hills, such as Bloody Ridge and Heartbreak Ridge in 1951 and White Horse Hill and Triangle Hill in 1952, and the line moved only a few kilometres.

chapters.title: The armistice line
arrows: Chinese offensive against the Kumsong salient
chapters.text: Fighting for outposts went on into 1953 while the talks resumed. In mid-July Chinese forces attacked the Kumsong salient in the centre and pushed the line back several kilometres. The armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 stopped the fighting where the armies stood: the front became the Military Demarcation Line, inside a demilitarised zone 4 km wide, and no peace treaty followed.
